Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - API usage, tool use, Anthropic SDK usage. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

content:
Belangrijk bericht in een ander openstaand venster, lees dit en geeft feedback en pas toe zo nodig:
Hier is een bericht dat je rechtstreeks in dat andere gesprek kunt plakken. Het is geschreven aan de assistent daar, met concrete technische ankers zodat het niet opnieuw fout kan gaan.
Belangrijk — lees dit voor je nog iets aan `launch.html` of `flow.html` wijzigt of merget.
Dit project (`tiro-health/jyz-pacs-test`, deployt naar radiology.tiro.health via GitHub Pages) heeft een radiology-calculator-feature die essentieel is en niet mag verdwijnen. In een parallel gesprek werd deze feature al twee keer per ongeluk volledig gewist doordat `launch.html` en `flow.html` in hun geheel werden overschreven met een oudere versie die de calculator-code niet bevatte. Dat moest telkens handmatig hersteld worden. Graag jouw hulp om dat definitief te voorkomen.
Wat de calculator-feature inhoudt (mag NOOIT verwijderd worden):

* `calculators.js` bevat `window.RADCALC` (39 calculators, pure data + logica + SVG). Dit bestand is de single source of truth en moet geladen blijven in `launch.html` via `<script src="calculators.js"></script>` (net na de tiro-web-sdk script-tag).
* In `launch.html`: de globale state `window._flowCalculators`, de functie `_syncCalculatorWindow`, de calculator-checkboxes onder de divider "AI en Calculatoren" (`#calc-templates`), het volledige calculator-venster (`#calc-picker`, `#calc-inputs`, `#calc-result`, `#calc-actions`, `#calc-copy`, `#calc-send`) en de 🧮-knop in het PiP-venster.
* In `flow.html`: de "Calculatoren"-sectie per onderzoekstype in de bewerk-slide-over (`add-calculator-btn`, `#calculators-list`), de "🧮 Calculatoren"-catalogusmodal, en `autoLinkCalculators` mét de galblaas-fix (`calcGalblaasFix_v1`).

De oorzaak van het wissen: er werd gewerkt op een verouderde `main` en vervolgens werden hele bestanden vervangen in plaats van gerichte wijzigingen te maken. Daardoor werd al het parallelle werk (waaronder de calculator) overschreven.
Concrete werkafspraken vanaf nu:

1. Synchroniseer eerst met de laatste `main` vóór je begint of iets merget:

```
git fetch origin main
```

`git rebase origin/main        # of: git merge origin/main`
Werk nooit verder op een branch die achterloopt op `main`.
2. Vervang nooit `launch.html` of `flow.html` in hun geheel. Maak uitsluitend gerichte, kleine edits in de secties die je echt nodig hebt. Overschrijf geen volledige bestanden en plak geen complete oude versie terug.
3. Controleer vóór elke commit/merge dat de calculator intact is. Snelle check:

```
grep -c 'calculators.js' launch.html      # moet ≥ 1 zijn
```

`grep -c '_flowCalculators' launch.html    # moet ≥ 1 zijn`
`grep -c 'AI en Calculatoren' launch.html  # de divider moet blijven`
`grep -c 'autoLinkCalculators' flow.html   # moet ≥ 1 zijn`
Als een van deze `0` teruggeeft, ben je bezig de calculator te wissen — stop en rebase eerst.
4. Bij een merge-conflict in deze twee bestanden: los het conflict op door beide kanten te behouden (jouw wijziging én de calculator-code), niet door één kant weg te gooien.

Kort samengevat: eerst rebasen op de laatste `main`, alleen gerichte edits, en vóór elke merge even checken dat `calculators.js` nog geladen wordt. Dan blijven jouw wijzigingen én de calculator naast elkaar bestaan.
Wil je dat ik er ook de beschermende CI-check bij zet (die een merge automatisch blokkeert zodra `calculators.js` niet meer geladen wordt)? Dan is het niet meer afhankelijk van of het andere gesprek de afspraken volgt.
Mss kan ik in dat gesprek best ook laten controleren op eventuele conflicten tov het besprek in dat venster en jouw aanpassingen momenteel gepushet?
Goed idee — dat is precies de juiste reflex. Hier is een extra stuk dat je onderaan het bericht kunt plakken. Zo laat je dat gesprek expliciet nagaan of hun werk botst met wat er nu op `main` staat.
Extra: controleer je werk tegen wat er nu al op `main` staat.
Er zijn zojuist wijzigingen naar `main` gepusht en gedeployed (de herstelde calculator-feature, merge-commit `cdb7b654`, PR #339). Voordat je verder werkt of iets merget, ga na of jouw lokale werk hiermee in conflict is:

1. Haal de laatste `main` op en vergelijk:

```
git fetch origin main
```

`git log --oneline origin/main -5          # zie je cdb7b654 (Restore radiology calculator feature)?`
`git diff --stat HEAD origin/main          # welke bestanden lopen uiteen?`
2. Kijk specifiek of jouw branch achterloopt op `main`:

```
git rev-list --left-right --count HEAD...origin/main
```

Het tweede getal = aantal commits dat op `main` staat maar niet bij jou. Is dat > 0, dan werk je op een verouderde basis — eerst rebasen (`git rebase origin/main`) voor je iets doet.
3. Doe een test-merge zónder te committen, om conflicten te zien:

```
git merge --no-commit --no-ff origin/main
```

Krijg je conflicten in `launch.html` of `flow.html`, los ze dan op door beide kanten te behouden (jouw wijziging én de calculator-code). Wil je de test terugdraaien: `git merge --abort`.
4. Bevestig na afloop dat de calculator nog intact is met de grep-checks hierboven (`calculators.js`, `_flowCalculators`, `AI en Calculatoren`, `autoLinkCalculators`).

Zo zie je meteen of jouw wijzigingen botsen met de herstelde calculator, en kun je ze veilig samenvoegen in plaats van er overheen te schrijven.
Zeg me gerust als je wil dat ik dit nog compacter maak of samenvoeg tot één doorlopend bericht.

input.head: claude/inspiring-hawking-a4v09g
input.body:
## Samenvatting

Vervangt de vlakke "Department template" en "Gebruiker template override" velden in het edit-paneel door inklapbare secties met radio buttons — precies zoals de gewenste UI-screenshot toont.

**Afdeling sectie:**
- Collapsible `<details>` met badge die de actieve modus toont (Textueel/Template)
- "Template standaardverslag" tekstveld (tiro:// URL)
- "Textueel standaardverslag" knop (opent code-editor)
- Radio buttons **Actief: ○ Template ○ Textueel** → slaat op als `deptMode`

**Gebruiker override sectie:**
- Zelfde structuur met radio buttons → slaat op als `userMode`
- Badge toont "geen override" / "override" / "Textueel"

**JS-wijzigingen:**
- `openEditor()` leest `et.deptMode` en `et.userMode` en vult radio buttons + badges in
- `save-edit-btn` slaat `deptMode`, `userMode` en `userTextTemplate` op bij Opslaan

Voegt een volledige **radiologie-calculatoren**-feature toe aan radiology.tiro.health. Netto 3 gewijzigde bestanden t.o.v. `main`: `calculators.js` (nieuw), `flow.html`, `launch.html`.

> ℹ️ De twee eerder besproken items (PiP send-to-dictation-fix + type-onderzoek → HOOFDLETTERS in de verslag check) staan **al op `main`** en zitten dus niet in deze diff.

## Wat deze PR toevoegt

**`calculators.js` (nieuw, single source of truth — `window.RADCALC`)**
- Catalogus van **39 calculatoren** (volumes, RADS-systemen, trauma, scores) met per calc: `inputs[]`, `compute()` en `triggerKeywords[]`. Puur data + logica, geen DOM.
- Zelf-gegenereerde schematische **SVG-figuren** (`svg()`) voor de visuele pickers — eigen tekeningen, geen externe/auteursrechtelijke beelden.

**`flow.html`**
- Nieuwe **"Calculatoren"-sectie** per examentype (analoog aan AI-regels): kies uit de catalogus + optionele Tiro-template-URL.
- `autoLinkCalculators()`: koppelt logische calculatoren automatisch aan examentypes op naam + modaliteit (17 types), eenmalig gemigreerd in `flowConfig_v1`.

**`launch.html`**
- Gekoppelde calculatoren verschijnen als checkbox in "Actieve template" (a) automatisch op basis van examentype, (b) via tekstscan-detectie → niet-invasieve toast die de calc activeert.
- **Calculator-venster**: live-berekend resultaat met "Kopiëren" + "↑ naar dictaat" en optioneel "Open Tiro-template".
- Nieuw invoertype **`visual-select`**: klikbaar figuurraster i.p.v. dropdown.

## Klinische verificatie

- **10 RADS-systemen exact 1-op-1 geverifieerd** tegen aangeleverde bronnen (ACR/AAST/SSR/RSNA/Radiopaedia): Lung-RADS v2022, O-RADS US v2022, CAD-RADS 2.0, Bone-RADS, TI-RADS, LI-RADS v2018, NI-RADS, PI-RADS v2.1, C-RADS v2023, Bosniak 2019 — plus SINS (alignement-fout gecorrigeerd) en AO Spine (TL/subaxiaal/hoog-cervicaal).
- **Accuraatheidsaudit** van de overige calculatoren tegen gezaghebbende bronnen: PESI, Villalta, mIBG Curie, adrenal washout/chemical-shift, leversteatose, Vauthey SLV, pediatrische miltlengte (Rosenberg), testis (Lambert 0,71) — allemaal bevestigd (2 precisie-tweaks doorgevoerd).

## Visuele pickers (klikbare figuren)

AO Spine thoracolumbaal (9, incl. benige B2/B3), subaxiaal (13, incl. facet F1–F4), hoog-cervicaal (3 regio-iconen), Bosniak 2019 (11), Lung-RADS (7 noduletypes), TI-RADS (compositie + echogeniciteit + vorm). O-RADS US & CAD-RADS bewust tekstueel gelaten.

## Testen

- Alle `compute()`-functies getest in Node (39 calculatoren).
- Brede Playwright-doorloop `flow.html` → `launch.html`: auto-koppeling, calculator-venster + live berekening, kopiëren/naar-dictaat, `visual-select`-figuren + klik-berekening, tekstscan-toast + activeren, en regressie (bestaande autofill/verslag-check onaangetast). Geen JS-fouten.

## Bewust buiten scope (latere/aparte taken)

- AI-prefill van calculator-velden vanuit het dictaat (fase 2).
- Visuele pickers voor O-RADS US en CAD-RADS.

De calculator-integratie (`window.RADCALC` / `calculators.js`) verdween live van radiology.tiro.health omdat een parallelle commit `launch.html` en `flow.html` overschreef met een versie zónder de calculator-code. `calculators.js` bleef bestaan maar werd niet meer geladen of gebruikt.

Deze PR her-integreert de feature op de **huidige** main-versie van beide bestanden en behoudt alle bestaande inhoud — puur additief + het samenvoegen van enkele gedeelde functies. Geen enkele functie uit de parallelle wijzigingen (o.a. `userTextTemplate`/TEKST-templates) gaat verloren.

Voegt een volledige **radiologie-calculatoren**-feature toe aan radiology.tiro.health. Netto 3 gewijzigde bestanden t.o.v. `main`: `calculators.js` (nieuw), `flow.html`, `launch.html`.

> ℹ️ De twee eerder besproken items (PiP send-to-dictation-fix + type-onderzoek → HOOFDLETTERS in de verslag check) staan **al op `main`** en zitten dus niet in deze diff.

## Wat deze PR toevoegt

**`calculators.js` (nieuw, single source of truth — `window.RADCALC`)**
- Catalogus van **39 calculatoren** (volumes, RADS-systemen, trauma, scores) met per calc: `inputs[]`, `compute()` en `triggerKeywords[]`. Puur data + logica, geen DOM.
- Zelf-gegenereerde schematische **SVG-figuren** (`svg()`) voor de visuele pickers — eigen tekeningen, geen externe/auteursrechtelijke beelden.

**`flow.html`**
- Nieuwe **"Calculatoren"-sectie** per examentype (analoog aan AI-regels): kies uit de catalogus + optionele Tiro-template-URL.
- `autoLinkCalculators()`: koppelt logische calculatoren automatisch aan examentypes op naam + modaliteit (17 types), eenmalig gemigreerd in `flowConfig_v1`.

**`launch.html`**
- Gekoppelde calculatoren verschijnen als checkbox in "Actieve template" (a) automatisch op basis van examentype, (b) via tekstscan-detectie → niet-invasieve toast die de calc activeert.
- **Calculator-venster**: live-berekend resultaat met "Kopiëren" + "↑ naar dictaat" en optioneel "Open Tiro-template".
- Nieuw invoertype **`visual-select`**: klikbaar figuurraster i.p.v. dropdown.

## Klinische verificatie

- **10 RADS-systemen exact 1-op-1 geverifieerd** tegen aangeleverde bronnen (ACR/AAST/SSR/RSNA/Radiopaedia): Lung-RADS v2022, O-RADS US v2022, CAD-RADS 2.0, Bone-RADS, TI-RADS, LI-RADS v2018, NI-RADS, PI-RADS v2.1, C-RADS v2023, Bosniak 2019 — plus SINS (alignement-fout gecorrigeerd) en AO Spine (TL/subaxiaal/hoog-cervicaal).
- **Accuraatheidsaudit** van de overige calculatoren tegen gezaghebbende bronnen: PESI, Villalta, mIBG Curie, adrenal washout/chemical-shift, leversteatose, Vauthey SLV, pediatrische miltlengte (Rosenberg), testis (Lambert 0,71) — allemaal bevestigd (2 precisie-tweaks doorgevoerd).

## Visuele pickers (klikbare figuren)

AO Spine thoracolumbaal (9, incl. benige B2/B3), subaxiaal (13, incl. facet F1–F4), hoog-cervicaal (3 regio-iconen), Bosniak 2019 (11), Lung-RADS (7 noduletypes), TI-RADS (compositie + echogeniciteit + vorm). O-RADS US & CAD-RADS bewust tekstueel gelaten.

## Testen

- Alle `compute()`-functies getest in Node (39 calculatoren).
- Brede Playwright-doorloop `flow.html` → `launch.html`: auto-koppeling, calculator-venster + live berekening, kopiëren/naar-dictaat, `visual-select`-figuren + klik-berekening, tekstscan-toast + activeren, en regressie (bestaande autofill/verslag-check onaangetast). Geen JS-fouten.

## Bewust buiten scope (latere/aparte taken)

- AI-prefill van calculator-velden vanuit het dictaat (fase 2).
- Visuele pickers voor O-RADS US en CAD-RADS.

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

I need to create a parameterized function that can handle both department and user level templates, add the button to the Gebruiker section, and set up the corresponding hidden textarea for user template edits.

**Current HEAD:** Both elements are completely gone from the HTML. `updateSectionStatuses()` only updates `ai-section-status`, `calc-section-status`, `preset-section-status`. There is no live visual feedback for the dept/user configuration state in the section headers.

**Where:** flow.html, HTML around the Afdeling/Gebruiker `<details>` section headers; `updateSectionStatuses()` function at line 4535.

### 2. AI rule textueel TT editor button (`ai-tt-trigger`) removed — flow.html

**What existed at aa8d6ea:** Each AI rule row in `renderAiRules()` had a "Textueel standaardverslag" block with a button (class `ai-tt-trigger`, `data-i="${i}"`) showing an Actief/Inactief badge (`ai-tt-badge`). Clicking it called `openTtEditor(currentEditId, 'ai-' + btn.dataset.i)` to open the TT editor for that specific AI rule's `textTemplate`. The event wiring was at line 1426–1431 in aa8d6ea.

**Current HEAD:** The entire "Textueel standaardverslag" block is gone from the `renderAiRules()` HTML template. No AI rule row has any button to set a textueel template. `syncAll()` no longer saves `editAiRules[i].activeMode` (the `.ai-mode-radio` selector is removed from syncAll at line 4250). AI rules can no longer have a `textTemplate` set at all through the UI.

**Where:** flow.html, `renderAiRules()` starting at line 4186; `syncAll()` at line 4242.

---

### 3. `flowPill()` no longer shows textueel mode in exam type cards — flow.html

**What existed at aa8d6ea:** `flowPill(tiroUrl, textTpl, mode, icon, label)` showed "📝 textueel" (amber) when `activeMode === 'textueel' && textTpl`, and a neutral "(inactief)" label when only textTpl existed with no URL.

**Current HEAD:** `flowPill(url, icon, label)` only checks if `url` is truthy (Tiro URL). Any exam type with `deptMode:'textueel'` or `userMode:'textueel'` but no Tiro URL shows "—" in the card flow summary instead of "📝 textueel". The textueel status is invisible in the exam type list.

**Where:** flow.html, `flowPill()` function (was around line 1053 in old, now around line 3909 in HEAD). Called at lines ~3972 for both dept and user pills.

---

### 4. AI rules with textueel-only templates silently dropped in launch.html

**What existed at aa8d6ea:** `updateTemplatesFromFlow()` generated `flow:ai-txt:${match.id}:${i}` items for AI rules that had `rule.textTemplate`. These appeared as checkboxes labeled "- AI (textueel)" in the template picker. `_syncTextueleTemplate()` would then sync `window._flowTextTemplate` when the user toggled such a checkbox.

**Current HEAD:** `aiRules.forEach` at line 1531–1540 starts with `if (!rule.template) return;` — any AI rule without a `.template` URL is skipped entirely. Rules that have only a `textTemplate` (textueel-only rules from before PR #335) are silently dropped from the template picker. No `flow:ai-txt:` key is ever created. For existing saved data with `textTemplate` on AI rules, those entries are lost to the end user.

**Where:** launch.html, line 1532 (`if (!rule.template) return;`). The old code path that created `flow:ai-txt:` items was at aa8d6ea lines 1584–1589.

---

### 5. AI replace-rule textueel pre-selection logic removed — launch.html

**What existed at aa8d6ea:** `activeItemKey()` (inner function) checked `replaceRule.activeMode === 'textueel' && replaceRule.textTemplate` to pre-select the `flow:ai-txt:` item when the replace rule was in textueel mode. This ensured the correct checkbox was pre-checked on page load.

**Current HEAD:** `activeItemKey()` is gone. The AI replace rule pre-selection now only handles `.template`-based rules (`const hasReplaceAI = aiRules.some(r => r.action === 'replace_template' && r.template)`). Any replace rule with only a `textTemplate` is treated as if no replace rule exists, so it falls through to dept/user template pre-selection instead.

**Where:** launch.html, line 1505 (`const hasReplaceAI = ...`); the old `activeItemKey()` function was at aa8d6ea lines ~1521–1532.

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

This PR adds a floating popout window feature for the Magic Clipboard component, allowing users to detach it into a separate draggable panel while keeping the main interface intact.

## Key Changes
- **New popout button**: Added a "Pop out clipboard" button next to the Dictation heading with an expand icon
- **Floating panel UI**: Created a new fixed-position floating panel (`#clipboard-popout`) with:
  - Draggable header with title and close button
  - Scrollable body container for the clipboard content
  - Proper z-index and styling for dark/light modes
- **Popout/pop-in functionality**: Implemented JavaScript logic to:
  - Move the `tiro-magic-clipboard` element between the main panel and floating window
  - Toggle button state and aria-pressed attribute
  - Update button title based on current state
- **Drag-to-move interaction**: Added pointer event handlers to allow users to drag the floating panel by its header
  - Constrains movement within viewport bounds
  - Uses pointer capture for smooth dragging
- **Button layout fix**: Removed `ml-auto` class from the verslag check button to prevent layout conflicts with the new popout button

## Implementation Details
- Uses a comment node (`clipboardHome`) as a placeholder to remember where the clipboard component originated, enabling seamless restoration
- Drag implementation uses pointer events with proper capture/release handling
- The floating panel is initially hidden and positioned at `top: 80px; right: 24px` with fixed dimensions (430px × 680px)
- Both popout and pop-in operations properly manage CSS classes (`hidden`/`flex`) for visibility

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

## 3. "tekst:" recognition logic — lines ending in ":" get uppercased

**`launch.html`, lines 2681–2698:**

```js
const _EXAM_MODALITEIT = /^\s*(RX|CT|CTA|MR|MRI|MRA|NMR|ECHO|ECHOGRAFIE|US|DOPPLER|MAMMO|MAMMOGRAFIE|TOMOSYNTHESE|PET|PET-CT|SPECT|SCINTIGRAFIE|BOTSCAN|DEXA|DOORLICHTING|SCOPIE|ANGIO|ARTROGRAFIE|MYELOGRAFIE|HSG|IVU)\b/i;
// line 2681

function uppercaseExamHeadings(text) {                                    // line 2682
    if (!text) return text;
    return text.split('\n').map(line => {
        const trimmedEnd = line.replace(/\s+$/, '');
        if (/:$/.test(trimmedEnd) && _EXAM_MODALITEIT.test(line))         // line 2686
            return line.toUpperCase();
        return line;
    }).join('\n');
}

function extractCleanCorrection(text) {                                   // line 2692
    const cleaned = text
        .replace(/<del[^>]*>[\s\S]*?<\/del>/gi, '')   // remove deletions
        .replace(/<ins[^>]*>([\s\S]*?)<\/ins>/gi, '$1') // keep insertions
        .replace(/<[^>]+>/g, '');                       // strip remaining tags
    return uppercaseExamHeadings(cleaned);              // line 2697 — applies the colon-heading rule
}
```

The logic: after stripping AI diff markup, any line that (a) ends with `:` and (b) starts with a known imaging modality keyword is converted entirely to uppercase. This is applied to the corrected text coming back from the AI verslag check. It is NOT a template-selection mechanism — it is a text formatting/normalization step that preserves the `CT THORAX:` / `MR LUMBALE WERVELZUIL:` heading style in the final output.

function applyFlowMatch(match) {                                           // line 1496
    showFlowStatus(null);
    const items = [];

    // Priority logic:
    // - gebruiker replaces afdeling (afdeling unchecked when gebruiker exists)
    // - first AI replace_template unchecks gebruiker and is checked instead
    // - additional AI add_template rules are always checked (stack on top)    (lines 1500–1503)

    const aiRules    = match.aiRules || [];
    const hasReplaceAI = aiRules.some(r => r.action === 'replace_template' && r.template);
    const hasUser    = !!match.userTemplate;
    const deptTextActive = match.deptMode === 'textueel';                  // line 1508
    const userTextActive = match.userMode === 'textueel';                  // line 1509

    if (match.deptTemplate) {
        const key = "flow:dept:" + match.id;
        TEMPLATES[key] = match.deptTemplate;
        items.push({ name: key, label: ..., checked: !deptTextActive && !hasUser && !hasReplaceAI });  // line 1513
    }
    if (match.textTemplate) {
        const key = "flow:dept-txt:" + match.id;
        TEMPLATES[key] = '__textueel__';
        items.push({ name: key, ..., checked: deptTextActive && !hasUser && !hasReplaceAI, mode: 'textueel' }); // line 1518
    }
    if (match.userTemplate) {
        TEMPLATES["flow:user:" + match.id] = match.userTemplate;
        items.push({ ..., checked: !userTextActive && !hasReplaceAI });    // line 1523
    }
    if (match.userTextTemplate) {
        TEMPLATES["flow:user-txt:" + match.id] = '__textueel__';
        items.push({ ..., checked: userTextActive && !hasReplaceAI, mode: 'textueel' }); // line 1528
    }
    aiRules.forEach((rule, i) => {
        const isReplace = rule.action === 'replace_template';
        const checked   = isReplace ? !replaceUsed : true;                 // line 1536
        if (isReplace) replaceUsed = true;
        items.push({ name: "flow:ai:"+match.id+":"+i, ..., checked });
    });

    // Store text templates for AI prompts + backup display
    window._flowTextTemplate = match.textTemplate || '';                   // line 1555
    window._flowUserTextTemplate = match.userTextTemplate || '';
    window._flowPresetText = match.presetText || '';
    window._flowLabelsDefaultVisible = match.labelsDefaultVisible === true;

    setDynamicTemplates(items);                                            // line 1578
    createTemplateForms();
}
```

`setDynamicTemplates(items)` injects the template checkboxes into the "Actieve template" panel. Each item with `checked: true` is the initially-active template form loaded via the Tiro Web SDK.

- **Lines 4094–4115** (`openEditor`): restores the radio buttons and badges when editing.
- **Lines 4632–4656** (`updateSectionStatuses`): keeps the badge labels "Template" / "Textueel" / "Override" / "geen override" in sync live while editing.

**In `launch.html` (the runtime)** — `applyFlowMatch` reads these stored values:

const userTextActive = match.userMode === 'textueel';    // line 1509

const hasUser = !!match.userTemplate || !!match.userTextTemplate; // was: alleen userTemplate

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.
